summary: A single-day working session turning a hand-edited per-client WordPress Docker Compose file into a reusable, parameterised stack deployable from Portainer on a phone. It covered env-var abstraction, two Portainer/Compose failures around volume naming, a small Flask container that generates .env files with random passwords, and a pivot to Git-repository-backed stacks. It closed with a debugging detour on zero-width Unicode characters introduced by copy-pasting code out of the chat.

findings.title: Environment variable substitution in Docker Compose volume names under Portainer
findings.body:
Portainer's Compose validator rejects environment variable substitution used as a *key* in the top-level `volumes:` block. A file containing

```yaml
volumes:
  ${PROJECT_NAME}-db:
  ${PROJECT_NAME}-wp:
```

fails validation with `validating /data/compose/<id>/docker-compose.yml: volumes Additional property ${PROJECT_NAME}-db is not allowed`. Substitution in `container_name`, in service `environment:` values and in port mappings is accepted — the restriction is specific to volume keys.

The supported alternative (Compose 3.6+) is a fixed key with a dynamic `name:` field:

```yaml
volumes:
  db-data:
    name: "${PROJECT_NAME}_db_data"
  wp-data:
    name: "${PROJECT_NAME}_wp_data"
```

This passes validation, but it only produces a valid volume if the variable actually resolves at deploy time. When `PROJECT_NAME` was empty, the name collapsed to `-wp` and the daemon refused it: `create -wp: "-wp" includes invalid characters for a local volume name, only "[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]" are allowed`. Docker local volume names must begin with an alphanumeric character, so a leading separator from an unset variable is a hard failure rather than a silent default. Using `_` as the separator instead of `-` does not solve the underlying problem — it only changes which invalid string is produced.

findings.title: Git-repository stacks over Portainer custom templates for per-client WordPress instances
findings.body:
For deploying one parameterised WordPress + MariaDB stack repeatedly for different clients, Portainer's Custom Templates proved too limited: the template environment-variable editor is basic, and variables were not reliably substituted into volume names at deploy time, producing invalid volume names.

The chosen approach instead points a Portainer stack at a Git repository. The repository holds a single version-controlled `docker-compose.yml` using `${...}` placeholders throughout, plus an `env.example` documenting which variables are required with dummy values. Real `.env` files are never committed — `.env` goes in `.gitignore`, and the client-specific file is supplied to Portainer at deploy time. This keeps one authoritative Compose file, gives reproducible deployments and rollout of Compose changes by re-pulling the repo, and sidesteps the template env-var handling entirely.

The minimum viable repository is just `docker-compose.yml` and `env.example`; a README and `.gitignore` are useful but not required for the mechanism to work.

findings.title: Env-generator container for per-client WordPress stack credentials
findings.body:
A small Flask container was built to remove the manual step of inventing passwords for each new client WordPress instance. It serves one page: a text field for the client name, and on submit it renders a ready-to-copy `.env` block containing `PROJECT_NAME`, `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`, `MYSQL_DATABASE`, `MYSQL_USER`, `MYSQL_PASSWORD` and the host port. Passwords come from Python's `secrets` module (`secrets.token_urlsafe` or `secrets.token_hex`), not from a hand-rolled random generator.

The layout is three files — `app.py`, `Dockerfile`, and `templates/index.html` — built with `docker build -t env-generator .` and run detached with `docker run -d -p 5000:5000 env-generator`. Running it without `-d` holds the terminal because Flask's dev server stays in the foreground.

The motivating requirement was phone-based deployment: open the generator in a mobile browser, paste the generated block into Portainer, deploy. The container ships Flask's development server, which is acceptable for an internal single-user tool but is explicitly not a production WSGI setup. Storing generated credentials to a Google Sheet was considered and treated as convenient rather than secure; the alternative noted was a vault or an encrypted store.

findings.title: Finding zero-width Unicode characters in code pasted from a chat interface
findings.body:
Code copied out of a chat interface can carry invisible characters — most commonly the zero-width space, U+200B, encoded as the bytes `e2 80 8b`. These survive into files and break parsers in ways that look impossible, because the offending character does not render.

Two characteristic symptoms: Docker reports `dockerfile parse error on line 2: unknown instruction: ​WORKDIR (did you mean WORKDIR?)` — the instruction is correct but preceded by a hidden character — and Python reports `SyntaxError: invalid non-printable character U+200B` pointing at an apparently blank line.

nano has no mode for displaying non-printing characters, so it cannot be used to diagnose this. Use `cat -v <file>` to render control and non-ASCII characters visibly, or `hexdump -C <file>` for the exact bytes. The fix is to delete and manually retype the affected lines, including blank ones, since the character often hides on lines that appear empty. Pasting through a plain-text editor before saving strips the problem at source.

The same class of corruption affects code pasted into rich-text web editors such as SharePoint pages, which may add smart quotes and zero-width characters on top of mangling indentation. Preformatted or code-snippet blocks avoid the rewriting; where a page only supports rich text, linking to the file in Git is more reliable than pasting it inline.

findings.title: Build context for Portainer stacks built from a Dockerfile
findings.body:
Portainer has no "working directory" setting for stack builds. When a stack's Compose file uses `build: .`, the path is resolved on the filesystem the Docker daemon sees, not against anything Portainer uploads — Portainer does not transfer the project files. If the source is already on the Docker host, give `build:` an absolute path (for example `build: /srv/env-generator`) rather than `.`, since the relative path has no meaningful base.

This only works where Portainer manages a local Docker socket. A remote Portainer agent cannot see the host's project directory unless specifically configured, in which case the workable routes are to build the image manually on the host (`docker build -t <name> .`) and reference it by image name in the stack, or to push it to a registry and pull from there. Either way the container remains manageable from Portainer's Containers view.

open_questions: Did the Git-repository stack in Portainer actually accept an uploaded .env file at deploy time, and did the ${PROJECT_NAME} volume names resolve correctly that way?
Was the volumes `name:` approach ever confirmed working, or abandoned untested after the empty-variable failure?
Where do generated credentials ultimately get stored — the Google Sheet idea was raised but never decided or implemented.
How to reliably paste code into SharePoint without invisible-character corruption; the code-snippet web part was suggested but not confirmed available on his pages.
Whether the env-generator should also emit a fully hard-coded per-client Compose file, which he raised at turn 17 and never returned to.
